quests.hint: To construct something again. The prefix means 'again', and the verb it joins is one you know.
quests.explanation: The prefix re- joins a base with no change: re + build. The base keeps every letter, including its final d.

quests.hint: A look at something before it is released. The prefix means 'before'.
quests.explanation: Pre- means 'before' and joins the base with no change: pre + view. The base keeps every letter, including its w.

quests.hint: To run a tape back to the start. The prefix means 'again', and the base is a verb that rhymes with 'kind'.
quests.explanation: Re + wind: in the verb wind (/waɪnd/), the i is long even though a short-vowel pattern would suggest otherwise. Several words with -ind work this way: find, kind, mind.

quests.hint: Not willing to wait. The 'not' prefix changes its last letter before this base.
quests.explanation: The prefix in- turns into im- before p, b or m: impatient, impossible, immature. The ending -tient is pronounced /ʃənt/ and is spelled the same as in 'patient'.

quests.hint: Against the law. The 'not' prefix takes on the first letter of the base.
quests.explanation: The prefix in- becomes il- before l, which creates a double l: in + legal gives illegal. The letters match, so the doubled consonant is a real feature of the spelling.

quests.hint: Not following a normal pattern. The same 'not' prefix, now matching the letter r.
quests.explanation: In- becomes ir- before r: in + regular gives irregular, with a double r. The last syllable is unstressed and written -ar, not -er.

quests.hint: Late for payment or return. The first part means 'above' and the second is a word ending in a silent e.
quests.explanation: Over + due: the prefix is a full word and joins without change. The final -ue in due is a common spelling for the long /uː/ or /juː/ sound: due, blue, clue.

quests.hint: Below the surface. The first part means 'below' and the second describes what you walk on.
quests.explanation: Under + ground: nothing is dropped. The ou in ground says /aʊ/, as in round, sound and found.

quests.hint: To put something somewhere and forget where. The prefix means 'wrongly'.
quests.explanation: Mis + place: the silent e stays in the base, and it is what keeps the c soft. Losing the e would make it look like a hard c.

quests.hint: Comparing size. The short base word has one short vowel and one final consonant.
quests.explanation: Doubling applies to -er as well as -ing and -ed: big becomes bigger, hot becomes hotter. The rule is the same one for all vowel-first endings.

quests.hint: The least difficult. The base ends in y, and the ending is -est.
quests.explanation: After a consonant, the y changes to i before -est: easy becomes easiest. The ea in the first syllable spells a long e.

quests.hint: More pleasant. The base already ends in e, so only one letter is added.
quests.explanation: A base ending in silent e takes only -r or -st: nice becomes nicer and nicest. A second e would make 'niceer', which never happens.

quests.hint: A card asking you to a party. Its verb ends in a silent e, and the noun ending is a familiar -tion chunk.
quests.explanation: Invite loses its e before -ation: invitation. Compare 'inform + ation', where there is no e to remove. The stressed syllable is ta.

quests.hint: Learning at school. The verb behind it ends in -ate.
quests.explanation: Educate loses its final e before -ion and becomes education. Many nouns from -ate verbs end in -ation (create, creation), and this one follows the same look.

quests.hint: Facts and data. The verb behind it has an r in the middle that people often forget.
quests.explanation: Inform + ation: nothing changes in the base, so the r must appear: infor-ma-tion. A frequent error is the spelling 'infomation', which leaves the r out.

quests.hint: Known to many. The noun 'fame' is the base.
quests.explanation: Silent e drops before -ous: fame becomes famous, not 'fameous'. The e survives only when a soft c or g needs it, as in courageous.

quests.hint: Likely to cause harm. It is built from a noun with an e already in the middle.
quests.explanation: Danger + ous: the base is kept whole, so the e stays after the g. Dropping that e gives 'dangrous', which is wrong.

quests.hint: Wanting to learn more. Three vowels sit at the end.
quests.explanation: The ending -ious is very common in adjectives: curious, various, obvious. The i is part of the suffix and the ending is said /iəs/.

quests.hint: Relating to songs. The noun 'music' plus an adjective ending.
quests.explanation: Music + al: the base is unchanged, and the /k/ sound stays written c: musical, not 'musikal'. The suffix -al makes an adjective.

quests.hint: Powered by current. The final /k/ sound is spelled with one letter.
quests.explanation: The suffix -ic is common on adjectives and it spells the /k/ with c: electric, plastic, classic. There is no k at the end.

quests.hint: Useful in real situations. It ends with a suffix that has the same /k/ spelling as in 'electric', followed by al.
quests.explanation: Many adjectives end in -ical: practical, typical, logical. The /k/ is written with c and the last syllable is a weak -al.

quests.hint: Where you sleep. Two short words, and the second has a double vowel.
quests.explanation: Bed + room is a closed compound: no letters change, and no space or hyphen is needed. The oo is the same as in 'moon' and 'food'.

quests.hint: Where planes land. The first part is what planes fly through, and the second part means a harbour.
quests.explanation: Air + port: air uses the vowel team ai. Compounds like this keep every letter of both parts and are written as one word.

quests.hint: A book for jotting things down. The first part is a short message, and the second is where you write.
quests.explanation: Note + book keeps the silent e in note, since the compound doesn't change either part. The e is what makes the o long.

quests.hint: To carry across. The prefix means 'across', and the root means 'carry'.
quests.explanation: Trans + port: from Latin trans (across) and portare (to carry). The same root gives import, export, portable and porter.

quests.hint: Regard for others. The root means 'look', and the word ends in a consonant cluster.
quests.explanation: Re + spect: the root spect (Latin specere, to look) is also in inspect and spectator. It ends in -ct, and both letters count.

quests.hint: To say what will happen before it does. The prefix is the same as in 'preview'.
quests.explanation: Pre + dict: the root dict (Latin dicere, to say) appears in dictate, dictionary and verdict. Predict means literally 'say beforehand'.

quests.hint: Too amazing to accept. It has three word-parts, and the middle one contains ie.
quests.explanation: Un + believe + able: the e of believe drops before -able (believable), but the word keeps the ie from believe. Compare receive, where it is ei after c.

quests.hint: The opposite of agreement. The prefix means 'not', and the base word keeps both e's.
quests.explanation: Dis + agree + ment: agree keeps ee because -ment begins with a consonant, so nothing is dropped. Three parts, three clear chunks.

quests.hint: Having achieved the goal. The base has two doubled letters, and the suffix has a single l.
quests.explanation: Success + ful: the base keeps cc and ss, and the suffix -ful has only one l: suc-cess-ful. Both doubles come from the base.
